extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in Christian apologetics, cultural criticism, and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive, literary essay defending Christian orthodoxy and arguing for its cultural, moral, and psychological value; uses examples, polemic, and analogies to make philosophical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping contrary passions side by side
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity allows seemingly inconsistent passions (optimism and pessimism, praise and denunciation) to coexist without collapsing into compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: St. Francis praising all good while St. Jerome denouncing all evil; the Church keeps these passions 'in their place' so each may be fully expressed without negating the other. Anti-pattern: reducing both to a muddled compromise (a 'dirty gray').

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of coexistent virtues (not mixture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity seeks to keep two colours coexistent but pure (analogy: shot silk or the red and white on St. George's shield), rather than mixing them into a weak blend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating virtues as mere gradations that blend into one another (e.g., letting red and white become a pink compromise). Value is in maintaining distinct, vibrant moral emphases simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic, monumental moral expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthodoxy permitted and cultivated heroic, theatrical forms of morality — extreme acts that are both terrible and attractive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: monkish fierceness scourging kings, St. Catherine kissing a criminal's bloody head. Modern anti-pattern: mild, reasonable reformers who write for prison reform but do not enact or embody dramatic moral gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed balance across a civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and cultural balances were often distributed across different people, regions, or institutions, creating an overall equilibrium for the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: northern ascetic practices enabling southern festival joy; balance of national characters (Germany vs France) producing European equipoise. Anti-pattern: enforcing uniformity that loses these compensatory functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict definition of doctrine to safeguard liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine had to be precisely defined; small doctrinal slips could lead to catastrophic social and spiritual consequences, so strict limits were necessary to preserve broader human liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: doctrinal precision prevented one idea from overpowering others and thereby damaging social practices (e.g., wrong phrasing could 'stop all the dances'). Anti-pattern: lax or vague doctrine that allows large-scale error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthodoxy as perilous and exciting, not merely safe
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthodoxy is not humdrum conservatism but a perilous, daring equilibrium requiring skill to maintain — sanity that is more dramatic than madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagery: a man controlling madly rushing horses yet retaining statuary grace. Anti-pattern: equating orthodoxy with dull respectability or mere safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of paradox as a positive moral method
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuing paradox (e.g., lion lying down with the lamb without losing ferocity) as a method to encompass complex human virtues rather than reducing or eliminating paradox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to retain the integrity of both elements in paradox instead of absorbing one into the other. Avoid interpretations that mean one side merely becomes like the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of exceptions and subtleties in life
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian doctrine is praised for not only finding general moral laws but for anticipating and providing for human exceptions and eccentricities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: finding the distance one may be 'quite miserable' without making it impossible to be 'quite happy' — a psychological insight. Anti-pattern: simplistic universal rules that ignore human particularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for fixed ideals when pursuing reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective reform/revolution requires a fixed, stable ideal or vision toward which to shape the world; constantly changing ideals make practical progress fruitless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: the artist who keeps changing the sitter (bad) versus the one who keeps changing the ideal colour (worse). Reform implies form — a clear picture of the desired end is necessary for determined action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform implies form — distinguish reform from passive evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform is intentional shaping toward a particular image; evolution or progress as automatic unrolling is an inadequate metaphor for deliberate moral or political change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the language of reform (purposeful shaping) over evolution/progress when arguing for conscious improvement. Anti-pattern: claiming 'progress' as an impersonal tendency and expecting that to motivate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a stable standard to permit decisive action
rubrics_metrics.description: To act swiftly and decisively (e.g., to denounce or to reform), there must be at that moment an abstract, immutable sense of right and wrong; without such a standard sudden action is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a Revolutionist must 'draw it HERE' to strike; evolutionary ambiguity prevents prompt, effective action. Anti-pattern: perpetual doubt that neutralizes activism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of vague physical metaphors over precise abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern thinkers who rely on physical metaphors ('higher', 'upper man') evade stating clear abstract moral claims; strong thought requires bald, precise abstract language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example criticism of Nietzsche: using 'over-man' instead of stating explicit moral aims. Guidance: prefer clear terms like 'happier' or 'purer' to vague physical metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of unchecked free thought undermining freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: An overabundance of managed scepticism or shifting philosophies can pacify people and prevent substantive social or political liberation; constant change of vision stabilizes existing institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: workers becoming first Marxian then Nietzschean but remaining in factory servitude; anti-pattern: distributing sceptical literature as a means to keep the status quo intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between impersonal evolutionary trends and purposeful artistic ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple impersonal trends may produce uniform results (e.g., all bluer), but a complex, intentionally designed end (an artistic chiaroscuro) requires a personal designer; morality as a complex arrangement implies direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: arguments that treat moral 'progress' as automatic are inadequate where the desired end is an intricate arrangement of qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary theory cannot by itself specify moral prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwinism or evolutionary metaphors can be marshalled to support conflicting moral outcomes (either cruelty or sentimentality) and therefore do not provide a reliable moral guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion: moral reasoning requires roots outside mere naturalistic trend; use of evolution without an independent standard yields contradictory ethical prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christianity as an organizer of cultural plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: By tolerating and balancing diverse emphases, Christianity allowed Europe to remain a unity while fragmenting into distinct nations with complementary characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: permitting Germans to be reverent and French to be experimental produced a stabilising equipoise. Anti-pattern: centralizing or homogenizing impulses that destroy complementary national temperaments.
